title: Council Post: What Side Of The GPT Divide Is Your Organization On?
text:
Ian Gotts is the founder and CEO at Elements.cloud.
We are starting to see LinkedIn posts suggesting that AI/GPT is hype. To use Gartner’s Hype Cycle terminology, they are saying we are over the hump, The Peak Of Inflated Expectations, and headed into the Trough of Disillusionment.
But I believe they are missing the point. A little over a year ago, most people had never heard of GPT. Since then, the potential use cases have exploded. In just the last three months, we’ve seen an acceleration in the capabilities of GPT, with a boost in the efficiency and overall performance of certain tasks. Admittedly, these are quite narrowly scoped tasks. AI/GPT is not going to replace anyone’s jobs right now. It is a productivity enhancer.
Over the longer term, AI/GPT will disrupt jobs, companies and even industries. One quote that I heard recently summarizes this beautifully: “AI won’t take your job—someone using AI will.” If we think about the revolution that the iPhone created, then AI/GPT is in the flip-phone phase. It could only make calls and send texts. And look at the iPhone now. AI/GPT has the same potential.
My AI/GPT Intern
Too many people are looking at AI/GPT as “Google Search on steroids.” They are asking it questions and relying on its knowledge of the world. But sadly, the world it sees is full of biases and inaccuracies, which leads to hallucinations. But what AI/GPT is very good at is solving puzzles when you give it all the puzzle pieces. You use AI/GPT’s ability to understand natural language prompts, reason, analyze data and respond in a way we understand. In this scenario, the results are staggeringly good.
AI/GPT is a very fast intern, and when well delegated, it can be extremely effective. What is produced is a great start; but now it needs work. A lot of the heavy lifting was being done very quickly. The results are only as good as the way you have delegated: the prompts and the context.
Like Any Technology, AI Adoption Is Slow
What is interesting is that adoption at a corporate level is slow, but there is a clear understanding that companies need to catch up. The recent Cisco AI Readiness survey that asked questions of over 8,000 IT leaders found that 97% of organizations say the urgency to deploy AI-powered technologies increased, and 84% of organizations think AI will have a very significant or significant impact on their business. Salesforce’s Generative AI Snapshot Research Series is an ongoing study of over 4,000 full-time workers across industries. It found that 86% of IT leaders expect generative AI to play a prominent role in their organizations.
There are very real and natural fears about the power of AI/GPT and how it can be controlled. These concerns are echoed in the Salesforce survey data: 65% said they can’t justify implementing generative AI yet. IT decision-makers cited several barriers to using generative AI, including:
- New security threats to their data (71%).
- Employees lack the skills (66%).
- Integration with their tech stack (60%).
- Lack of a unified data strategy (59%).
I would add to this list that some organizations are tech-risk-averse. They don’t want to commit to tech innovation until it is clear who the market leaders are. That way, there is less risk of picking the wrong technology.
These are the Early Majority when you look at the classic buyer bell curve, made popular in Geoffrey Moore’s book Crossing the Chasm. Those who are engaging, experimenting and winning with AI/GPT are the Early Adopters. These may be organizations or certain individuals in organizations who are the Early or Late Majority. More on this later.
Employees Are Voting With Their Browsers
While many organizations are very hesitant to approve the use of AI/GPT in the workplace, their employees are seeing such a powerful ROI that they are ignoring the rules. This is putting both employees and their employers at security, reputational and regulatory risk. Organizations that are implementing a corporate-wide ban of AI/GPT, in my view, are shortsighted.
As a previous CIO at one of the largest U.K. government agencies, I understand the concerns. I remember back to when Salesforce launched and there was the same skepticism with the security of “cloud computing”—except it wasn’t called cloud computing back then.
At that time, I was the CEO of a tech company, and we were one of Salesforce’s earliest customers in the U.K. We saw the benefits of being an early adopter of cloud computing and worked to mitigate the risks that came with it. AI/GPT is the same. Now as CEO of Elements.cloud, we’ve been an early adopter because we need to be at the forefront of this revolution.
GPT Divide
We see three issues with organizations not running AI/GPT pilots and that have taken the view that it is banned until it matures:
- Stealth GPT: The ROI is so overwhelming for AI/GPT that individuals will use it under the radar (hence, “StealthGPT”).
- Innovation brain drain: The most innovative may choose to leave as they see the potential of AI/GPT and will be frustrated over not having that tool at their disposal.
- GPT divide: Organizations that embrace AI/GPT can accelerate their innovation, increase productivity and therefore be more competitive.
Executive Actions
Executives in every organization should approve the use of AI/GPT, if only in narrowly scoped, carefully controlled pilots. They need to staff those projects with individuals who are the most innovative and who are desperate to use AI/GPT to benefit their organizations.
Guardrails need to be in place to ensure data security and trust are not at risk. As a business leader, you need to accept that technology decisions may be wrong because the market leaders have not yet emerged. Understand that not every use case trialed will be right.
As a recent Harvard Business Review article notes, “Strategy, not technology, is the key to winning with GenAI.” Only by launching these pilots can executives shape the strategy that makes sure that their organizations land on the correct side of the GPT divide.

title: Quizlet Using AI As A Socratic Tool To Ask Better Questions
text:
In schools, 2023 was the year of generative AI-powered chatbots. Students suddenly found themselves with a tool that was always willing to provide answers, even if those answers were sometimes hallucinations or involved manufactured sources. The challenge in 2024 has been to move AI from being a powerful tool lacking clear direction to being a tool that can help students and educators achieve the goal of educating students regarding the underlying academic content and the effective use of emerging digital technologies. Quizlet sees the answer in helping students ask better questions.
Questions are the Answer
In August 2023, Quizlet released a new suite of AI tools, Magic Notes, which takes notes and repackages them in several ways, serving up flashcards, practice tests, and other interactive experiences designed to deepen and reinforce learning, and Q-Chat, which harnesses the conversational capabilities of generative-AI chatbots to provide students with a natural environment in which they can interact in a question-answer model with the AI, with the AI generating the questions and prompting the students for answers.
Uptake has been brisk over the past five months, with students generating over five million Magic Notes. However, the real star of the suite has been Q-Chat, with almost ten million conversations taking place.
Nitin Gupta, VP of Product at Quizlet, said, “Study behavior is more than just large language models and generative AI. At the end of the day, students don’t care about AI; they just care about getting their needs met.”
Meeting student needs is where Quizlet has a distinct advantage; Quizlet knows what students are trying to learn. Moreover, Quizlet knows the topics students are spending the most quizzing themselves on, and they also know what students find most challenging. This is valuable insight when it comes to building AI tools that can drive student learning. Efficient learning will always be about quickly discerning what students already know and then focusing on what they need to learn next as they progress from their current knowledge state to their ultimate destination.
By being a discursive partner rather than an oracle, Quizlet can assume the role of the Socratic guide, supplying students not with answers to questions they might have at any given moment but with questions that will help draw out the knowledge they seek.
Finding the right questions to ask is the biggest challenge. Without some model of the structure of what is being learned and some awareness of what a student knows, an instructor risks asking questions beyond the scope of being useful. The right question is sufficiently challenging to be interesting without being so simple as to be tedious or so complicated as to be frustrating. If the proper sequence of questions can be found, they will act like breadcrumbs, leading a student along a learning path.
Determining where students actually have difficulty in the learning process is not readily revealed by looking at exam results. Exam results may show where students are on their journey, but they do not provide insight into which parts of the trip went quickly and which went slowly. That requires attending to the learning process, and this is where Quizlet has some insight.
Aggregating study behavior across student populations provides deep levels of insight. By seeing where most students struggle, Quizlet can find particularly challenging areas or where the underlying presentation needs improvement. Determining whether difficulties lie in the material itself (something genuinely hard) or in the presentation of the material (something challenging to teach) or, in a class’s experience (this teacher finds the material hard to teach), or in a student’s readiness to learn the material (this student is not prepared), and so forth, all reflect subtle differences in experience that have markedly different causes and whose remediation requires different strategies. Because of its tight integration in the learning process, Quizlet is well-positioned to gather and utilize this information to improve learning across the board as it derives future product enhancements.
Traditional analysis methods would be challenged to capture this data, let alone sort through it. With the emergence of AI, not only is it possible to trawl through the old data, but the new tools can be iteratively improved as more data is collected. This ultimately makes Quizlet’s move from a self-study tool to an interactive Socratic tutor possible. Opening a dialogue and saying “Quiz me” creates new possibilities for student learning. It can ask questions intended to draw out student knowledge and identify things a student might be overlooking. An example would be saying, “People who try to learn X, Y, and Z usually also spend time studying A, B, and C.” The effort of humans trying to learn and the ability to analyze data on what humans do that leads to successful learning opens up dimensions beyond what is available in a pure language model.
To reach their full potential, these tools must be made teacher-friendly. They will need to be able to look under the hood and report back on what students are struggling with so that teachers can confidently look at the AI agent as an ally in teaching and not as an adversary sneaking in to do the work for the student. When done correctly, the AI agent will enable teachers to finally engage in the learning process and intervene at optimal learning. Quizlet is well situated to realize this potential.

title: Council Post: How To Handle The AI Ethics Dilemma In Your Business Development
text:
Vice President, Head of Digital Modalities at SAP.
It's incredible, really, how AI has transformed the way we do business—making things faster and more personalized and giving us insights we never thought possible. But as with any great power, there's a big responsibility that comes along with it—especially when we talk about ethics.
As a digital transformation leader, my career spans over 15 years at esteemed organizations in both Asia and North America, where I have led crucial AI-driven innovation and incubation initiatives aimed at boosting the productivity of sales & business development teams leading to incremental business impact. My experience across diverse cultures has honed my focus on thoroughness and precision to eliminate bias and achieve complete compliance, transparency and trust within an enterprise as we integrate AI into our work environments.
The Role Of AI Ethics In Sales & Business
Pulling from my vast experience in this area, I'd like to chat about what AI ethics means in the world of sales and business. First off, there's the big deal about data privacy. Sales AI tools are like sponges, soaking up all kinds of customer info. We have to make sure this data is kept safe and sound, respecting laws like GDPR in Europe or CCPA in California. Imagine if someone mishandled your personal info—not cool, right?
Then there's the issue of algorithmic bias. This is a tricky one. Sometimes, AI can make decisions based on data that's, well, a bit skewed. This means some customers might get unfairly treated, which is definitely not what we want. Fairness is key.
Transparency and accountability are also massive. We need to make AI’s decisions as clear as a sunny day. And if something goes wrong, we should know who's responsible and how to fix it. It's like having a roadmap for AI's decision-making process.
In the realm of sales and marketing, it's quite eye-opening to see the gap in consumer awareness regarding cyber risks and the emergence of deepfakes. Despite the considerable buzz surrounding these topics, it's startling to note that a significant portion of the audience—49% of consumers—appears relatively unconcerned about the use of generative AI in creating fake news stories.
How Businesses Can Navigate AI Ethics
So, how can businesses handle all this? First, you need to draw up some solid ethical guidelines for using AI. Think of it as setting ground rules for a game—what's in bounds and what's out? This includes making sure AI treats everyone fairly and has its hands clean when dealing with data. And it’s not just tech folks who should have a say in this. Legal teams, customer advocates—everyone should chip in to make these guidelines as strong and inclusive as possible. Our organization has set up an AI Steering Committee, which holds us accountable for addressing any dilemma around AI ethics and allows for diverse input.
Once your guidelines are in place, it's all about sticking to them. This means training the team regularly on ethical AI use. Just like how athletes train to stay in top form and how cars need regular check-ups, AI systems need audits to make sure they're following the rules and respecting everyone’s privacy.
Now, let's talk about being open with customers. Businesses should be like open books, telling customers exactly how they use AI—how they collect data, what they do with it, and how they keep it safe. This builds a bridge of trust, and customers can cross it knowing exactly what they’re getting into.
Dealing with algorithmic bias is another big chapter. This means using data that reflects all kinds of customers and constantly testing AI to make sure it's not biased. It's like having a diverse group of taste testers for a new dish to make sure it appeals to everyone.
In Summary
AI ethics isn’t something you just set and forget. It’s always evolving, always changing. Businesses need to stay on their toes, keeping up with the latest in AI tech and ethics. It’s like surfing—you need to stay balanced and ready to ride the next big wave. It's about striking a balance between leveraging cutting-edge technology and ensuring our audience is savvy to the realities of the digital world—a crucial aspect of responsible and effective sales and marketing in today's environment.
In wrapping up, navigating the world of AI ethics in sales and business development is about understanding the challenges, setting up the right path with clear guidelines, ensuring everyone follows this path, being transparent, keeping an eye out for biases and always being ready to learn and adapt. By doing all this, businesses can harness the power of AI while keeping their ethical compass pointing true north. This isn’t just about avoiding trouble; it’s about building a relationship of trust with customers that stands the test of time.
Finally, it's crucial to acknowledge that the secret ingredient behind successfully implementing the steps mentioned above is obtaining executive sponsorship within your organization. I am profoundly grateful for consistently receiving the required leadership support and partnership in my organization, both within our business unit and outside extended teams, which has been instrumental in making our AI programs successful. It is truly a collective effort and takes a village to make the magic happen!

title: Council Post: Is There A Tech Extinction Event Coming?
text:
Raphaëlle d'Ornano is the Managing Partner + Founder at D'Ornano+Co., a pioneer in Hybrid Growth Diligence.
Mass extinction events occur when 75% or more species are lost in a short period. The last two years signaled an end to an era of low interest rates, cheap capital and artificial growth conditions. High-growth tech (HGT) companies are now at an inflection point where their future is far from assured as they face harsher funding conditions.
In addition to being suddenly subject to macroeconomic forces from which they were previously insulated, a simultaneous wave of new technological threats (and opportunities) means they face a fundamental landscape shift to which they will have to adapt. In my experience only about 1 in 4 are currently set up to do so; the remaining 75% of these companies may begin to vanish in what could be a mass extinction event, both through "depressed" M&A or through collapses—starting with billion-dollar "unicorns" and all the "soon-icorns" in their trail.
It's hard to overstate the potential fallout. Per Pitchbook data, unicorn companies valued at over $1 billion account for about 7% of the U.S.'s gross domestic product (i.e., when measuring these unicorns' total last known valuation). Building these companies on unsustainable conditions has created a house of cards, where it's only a matter of time before it could come crashing down.
The potential implications for private and public market investors should not be understated.
On the one hand, the emergence of the internet, mobile technology, cloud computing, generative AI and other science-based technology has created impressive value for many HGT companies. On the other, these companies' business models and their rapid rate of change have outpaced investors' traditional analyses—leaving investors in uncertain, uncharted territory.
This uncertainty makes it tempting to dispense with traditional evaluation criteria, harkening back to the last decade's unsustainable growth mindset and high-risk tolerance. This is currently at play in generative AI with very high premiums, especially at the application level. But the further investors stray from the core principles of finance, the more they risk creating unrealistic assessments. Unrealistic assessments can lead to overestimations of value, poor investment returns and strategic errors.
The recent wave of investment in HGT companies fueled by low interest rates and FOMO led some venture capital and nontraditional investors to make mistakes that are now just starting to be recognized. The goal here is not to make them again while continuing to invest in HGT companies that naturally bear high risks. For some investors, such as buyout investors investing in VC-backed assets, this could be a time to consider gaining exposure to HGT companies. Established businesses that are putting new technologies front and center of their business models through M&A are also an option investors can consider.
Investors are faced with the twin challenges of avoiding companies that will not sustain the changing times and supporting those whose strong foundations leave them well-positioned for profound transformation.
If changed interest rates could be the catalyzing factor for an extinction event in tech, then generative AI, climate change and macro and geopolitical forces are the three meteors that threaten every company even when they prove to be resilient in a "steady-state" condition. All three factors could constitute a single point of failure, putting the entire business at risk.
One solution is to pressure test the evolutionary resiliency of HGT companies (both new and incumbent). This test should be performed during the pre-IPO round for those on the path to IPO.
Investors need to be able to see around corners in terms of long-term future trends and assess the durability of a company's business model. They can only do that if they have a firm grasp of the future economics (prospects of growth and profitability) of HGTs and their industries, with an understanding of key levers driving a company's intrinsic value and resilience. Building a conviction on the growth rate is central in the analysis as only growth has a compounding effect on valuation. Profitability comes second. Hence, investors should consider assessing growth by challenging the qualitative aspects of a company's revenue, growth, margins and balance sheet resilience that constitute the backbone for long-term growth.
Together, they form the foundation of a new methodology of analysis, advanced growth intelligence (AGI). AGI is a more thoughtful approach to looking at assets, especially those with higher technological and capex intensities. It is a more scientific lens through which to assess assets across the investment spectrum, from the high-risk, early-stage generative AI business—for which investors could be willing to pay 150 times or more annual recurring revenue (ARR)—to more mature online businesses and recently IPOed companies.
Beyond a clear understanding of the specific value levers of high-growth tech companies, AGI builds on pattern recognition (based on private and public sources), which can provide a more holistic view of growth and profitability trajectories. Success is not measured by handoffs from one investment silo to another, it's the ability to deliver value over the long term. It can and should be measured and benchmarked in a rigorous way.
By returning to investment first principles, AGI can help investors pressure test assets under real conditions to validate uncertain businesses' intrinsic value and resilience. Most importantly, it can help identify the right questions investors need to ask of disruptive assets to create a clearer picture of risk. Though volatility and uncertainty cannot be reduced, it can be understood.
While investors are up against challenging headwinds resulting from interest rates and single-point failure threats, a new approach to understanding high-growth tech companies could allow for investors to answer the most critical question: Do we want to make this investment?
Now could be the time for investors to course-correct, using rigorous, data-based assessments and business judgment to inform decisions and increase risk transparency. As new unicorns are poised to emerge with the current generative AI wave, this new approach has the potential to allow for sound investments in exciting opportunities.
Every extinction event clears the way for new ideas to emerge, but it's up to investors to identify which companies have what it takes to weather the storm of change and ride the wave of opportunity.

title: Council Post: AI's Current And Future Impacts On Construction
text:
Mark Schwartz is the Senior Vice President of Construction Enterprise Solutions at Trimble.
More than a year after the launch of ChatGPT, artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere, and its use is being explored across industries—including within typically technologically averse sectors like construction.
Far from being nervous about its applications, many contractors are embracing AI innovations, particularly given their potential to transform end-to-end workflows. From design and construction to operations and maintenance, AI is unlocking efficiencies and helping solve the labor shortage by automating repetitive tasks. It's optimizing projects and enabling them to be built more sustainably, and it's streamlining the supply chain—facilitating better relationships between contractors and project owners through enhanced predictability.
While AI used to only be within the domain of large companies due to high upfront costs, the democratization of technology mixed with the sheer number of companies working on developing new AI initiatives has made the costs dramatically decrease. Now, small and medium contractors can more easily afford to experiment with AI, making it much more accessible and impactful.
As we look ahead in 2024, below are a few ways that AI has already begun to make inroads in construction along with projections of how it will continue to positively impact the industry in the years to come.
Helping Solve The Labor Shortage
For the past decade or more, the labor shortage has been particularly acute in the construction industry, leading contractors to look for new solutions. This is one area in which AI has proved particularly helpful, as it can automate repetitive tasks while also reducing the human errors that naturally occur with things like data entry.
Now, instead of a human manually inputting information, data can be quickly scanned and exported into a format that's usable for multiple stakeholders. This is helpful for repetitive tasks associated with invoicing, order tracking, credit collections or reconciliations—freeing accounts receivable and accounts payable personnel to focus on more important, strategic initiatives.
AI is also helping to solve the labor shortage when it comes to design, as it's being used to harness and leverage data more efficiently—enabling designers to iterate faster and facilitate better decision-making. For example, architects can now leverage AI to quickly generate conceptual images and photorealistic visualizations of 3D models. This helps inspire the creative process, communicate their vision and build alignment faster.
When it comes to the actual constructibility of designs, AI is also working to automate repetitive actions for things like rebar detailing, which is less generative and more predictive. For example, AI can now suggest specific rebar layouts based on what a detailer has done previously, streamlining the design process. While this doesn't mean AI is building the actual building, it's being incorporated into various processes to simplify workflows and reduce overall decision-making and workload.
By augmenting the human experience, AI enables work to be done more efficiently and accurately, with manual checkpoints woven in to ensure the data is accurate. Because the data going out is only as good as the data being used to train the machine learning models that power AI, clean data and manual checkpoints overseen by a real person are imperative to the industry's trust in AI systems and their success overall.
Enhancing Sustainability
Construction is a major emitter of embodied carbon, causing many contractors and asset owners to look for new ways to mitigate their impact on the environment. This includes a concerted effort to reduce the carbon emissions associated with materials and construction processes throughout the lifecycle of a building. AI can enable contractors to become efficient and productive, which naturally translates to greater environmental benefits.
One example involves the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), which was looking to improve wall insulation across a large number of residential buildings. Instead of creating customized cladding panels for every vent, door and window, the walls were scanned using 3D laser scanning. AI was then used to extract the facade components from the data, and the dimensions were sent to panel manufacturers who produced them off-site. Without AI, the cost of delivering this project at scale wouldn't have been feasible.
Making The Supply Chain More Efficient And Effective
Amid market volatility and economic uncertainty, companies are also turning to AI to more accurately connect and orchestrate their supply chains. Doing so can improve efficiency and productivity while also creating a better customer experience.
Twenty years ago, many supply chain decisions for retail were based on "tribal knowledge." The sales manager guessed which goods people were going to buy, the logistics manager guessed the capacity needed to deliver goods to the customer, and the supplier guessed what demand would be in the coming months and tried to prepare accordingly. Careers were built off this methodology, which came with both successes and failures.
Today's supply chains are much more accurate because they're digitally interconnected, helping to take the guesswork out. From a construction perspective, this comes into play because contractors are often either storing supplies or waiting for supplies, which can lead to delays and cost overruns.
AI optimizes the supply chain by connecting the entire ecosystem and extrapolating data from it, helping more accurately predict when materials will be available. This can help keep projects on track, improving productivity and strengthening the contractor-to-project owner relationship by providing a sense of predictability.
As we've been hearing across the media landscape, AI is here to stay. While most people are aware of the digital-first uses of AI for things like ChatGPT and NFL analytics, AI has and will continue to transform traditional industries like construction as well.
However, the stakes are much higher, and the impact could be even greater as AI is used to change the nature of the physical world. This includes helping everyone from architects and designers to contractors and project owners more efficiently build and maintain our most important assets—from the homes we live in to the buildings we work and play in every day.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Trends And Use Cases To Follow In 2024
text:
Sunny Pokala, CEO, Amtex Systems.
Generative AI is poised for continued advancement in 2024.
According to McKinsey, the technology could contribute up to $4.4 trillion annually across 63 use cases. That said, most businesses are all only starting on their journey of understanding the possibilities, reach and power of generative AI.
There's no denying the excitement that surrounds generative AI. Many executives, though, favor a measured strategy, testing a small number of use cases and gathering more information before making large investments. Businesses will also have to assess if they have the requisite technological know-how, data infrastructure, operational framework and risk management for some of the more innovative uses of generative AI.
This article aims to help business experts consider how generative AI could create business value going forward by highlighting key areas that should see growth and development in the coming months and years. Here are a few trends to follow:
Quantum AI
Quantum AI, harnessing the tenets of quantum mechanics, signifies a substantial advancement beyond the confines of classical computing. Functioning with quantum bits (qubits), distinct from conventional bits, quantum AI leverages the unique capability of existing in multiple states concurrently, leading to exponential amplifications in processing power. This attribute empowers quantum AI to analyze and process extensive, intricate datasets at unprecedented speeds.
Multimodal AI Models
Notable progress in multimodal AI is poised to revolutionize creative capabilities. This evolution is exemplified by substantial language models such as Mistral, Llama 2 and GPT-4. Embracing diverse data types, popular models like GPT-4V and upcoming ones such as LLava are also designed to render artificial intelligence more dynamic and intuitive.
Small Language Models
In 2024, the prevalence of small language models (SLMs), trained on meticulously curated, high-caliber datasets, is expected to become standard practice. Characterized by fewer parameters and reduced system requirements, SLMs like Microsoft's PHI-2 and Mistral 7B can deliver performance suited to manage smaller tasks than their larger counterparts, large language models (LLMs).
Autonomous Agents In Generative AI
The landscape of generative AI is undergoing a profound transformation driven by autonomous agents incorporating multimodal AI and advanced algorithms. Leveraging cutting-edge tools such as LangChain and LlamaIndex, these autonomous systems exhibit self-learning capabilities, analyzing diverse datasets to derive informed conclusions.
Applications And Services Enhanced With Generative AI
According to a study conducted by AIM Research, 40% of enterprise applications will integrate conversational AI as a feature in 2024.
This is one example pointing toward the imminent trend where a substantial portion of application vendors—acknowledging the paramount importance of user engagement and experience—will actively incorporate AI into their offerings. Here are a few industries these developments could impact:
Healthcare
Generative AI will play a pivotal role in various aspects of the healthcare sector, ranging from generating synthetic medical images for model training to formulating personalized treatment plans. Its influence is anticipated to be instrumental in advancing healthcare technologies and diagnostics and, ultimately, elevating the standard of patient care.
Education
While the integration of AI in educational settings may initially encounter some hesitation, we will likely see the gradual acceptance of this technology.
Educators will likely progressively incorporate generative AI into various aspects of their pedagogical practices, employing it to generate notes, reports, lesson plans and summaries. Furthermore, its transformative influence will extend to creating personalized learning experiences.
Software Development
The advent of generative AI is also set to revolutionize software development through enhanced data collection and improved comprehension in interactions between analysts and clients. This advancement serves to mitigate the risks associated with miscommunication by enabling swift prototyping.
Additionally, generative AI streamlines the generation of code snippets in diverse languages, augmenting developer productivity and elevating software quality. This could have a huge impact on productivity.
Conclusion
The current transformation in the AI landscape is undeniably revolutionary, presenting a paradigm shift.
The significance of these advancements is underscored by the fact that 97% of respondents to an Accenture survey believe that AI is worthy of a long-term investment. Additionally, the same percentage of respondents believe that it will be transformative for their company and their industry. Leaders are actively exploring high-potential areas such as content generation, coding, software development, product development, customer service and IT operations for investment opportunities.
Still, this journey is not without its challenges. Companies must find strategic answers to the difficulties posed by generative AI, such as the ones mentioned in the introduction of this article: testing use cases and ensuring the organization is prepared with technological know-how, data infrastructure, operational framework and risk management necessary for success.
High-quality, diverse data is also essential, as are ethical considerations that have led to calls for stringent regulations. Ensuring compliance with rules, strong security measures and resource-intensive training will be crucial to overcoming these challenges.

title: Council Post: Protecting Human Intelligence With AI
text:
Chief Product Officer at Nasuni.
The tight labor market in the U.S. is accelerating a technical exodus. Skilled knowledge workers have more employment options, so more people are moving around to advance their careers. In the process, they are taking unique business and operations knowledge with them.
Yet that specialized human intelligence isn't entirely walking out the door. Some of it is left behind in structured and unstructured data, or what we all know as files. Enterprises have not had the tools to uncover and extract knowledge from this distributed data, but I believe this is going to change very soon.
Countering Technical Exodus
In my last few articles, I introduced a few essential steps organizations need to follow to prepare for the enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) tools of today and tomorrow. This piece is slightly more speculative but points to the sort of possibilities that may be available if you consolidate and curate your data. Imagine an enterprise AI solution capable of uncovering, collating and synthesizing the knowledge and history of employees, effectively creating a digital twin ready to share that person's key ideas and contributions.
Where would this tool find such information? Consider the output of a standard knowledge worker over the course of a year. They create and edit documents, spreadsheets and presentations. They correspond with colleagues, prospects and customers via email and messaging apps. Maybe they work in specialized design applications or comment on files in a platform like Microsoft Teams. There will be calendar notices, notes, videos and all kinds of back-and-forth within groups and departments.
The data the average person generates simply by working inside your organization is going to be incredibly diverse and widely distributed across different systems and applications. No former coworker of the departed employee is going to want to pull all that together—if you assign someone that task, you risk prompting another resignation. But if you consolidate all of your organization’s data in a way that makes it easily accessible to approved enterprise AI tools, then the diverse, distributed nature of this data is no longer an obstacle. After consolidation and curation, those scattered digital breadcrumbs become easily accessible to AI.
Preserving Human Intelligence
I don't believe the virtual representation of a departed worker’s knowledge would be a digital twin in the sense that it could perform that person's job. However, this specialized AI tool could represent a departed worker's knowledge, generating information from their past work data. This approach could assist in onboarding new hires by providing summaries of predecessors' contributions, accelerating the learning process.
In an engineering firm, for example, the tool could consolidate complex renderings and digital models, aiding new hires in navigating previous projects efficiently. Beyond engineering, this concept could benefit various industries by acting as an internal research assistant, enabling easy access to past employees' work-related content, and benefiting both new and existing team members.
Investing In Data Stewards
To make this work, an organization will need relevant data to train the AI tool, which will in all likelihood be a large language model (LLM). You don't want to expose this tool to old and outdated files and information, so you will have to curate the data associated with the individual who has left the organization. If you feed AI tools outdated data, they will generate outdated results. Curation is critical if you want useful, relevant output.
There are various data intelligence tools available to help curate unstructured data and ensure the data that you feed into an LLM is timely and accurate. These tools provide information about the unstructured data in your environment. Another tool to consider is a sophisticated search engine that will index the data based on its content and allow administrators to query the resulting index to identify the most relevant content. Be sure to experiment with data intelligence tools and search tools to find the ones that meet technical and financial requirements.
The final piece necessary to institute this sort of system would be human talent. Data consolidation and curation tools will get you ready to leverage AI, but organizations will need to invest in data stewards responsible for understanding the different data types and the relevancy and recency of data. You will still need people to make the critical decisions and ensure that you're leveraging the right data.
This process is typically referred to as the "human in the middle." As stated previously, results generated by AI tools are only as good as the data that they have available. In most cases, organizations will want to have humans verify the results generated by AI tools for accuracy and the absence of bias or hallucinations. This "human in the middle" concept will ensure that the results generated from a previous employee's work product will be usable by those who take on that individual's tasks.
Final Thoughts
This will all require some work, but the long-term rewards will be significant. By consolidating and curating your data and then building and maintaining a team of data stewards who intelligently manage that data, you will be setting your organization up for the AI tools of the future—the knowledge tool described here or one of the many other exciting solutions yet to come. I suspect you will also reduce the risk of technical exodus, as you will be building the kind of company that people do not want to leave in the first place.

title: Top 5 High-Income Skills In Tech In 2024, According To Indeed
text:
There's a new wave of employers following a trend that's rapidly gaining in popularity and effectiveness: skills-based hiring.
Even Big Tech names such as LinkedIn, Google and IBM, traditionally associated with hiring Ivy League graduates, are embracing hiring according to skills and culture compatibility, thus widening and ensuring diversity in their talent pools. While many employers are switching over to skills-based hiring and are becoming more vocal in their stance on candidates with transferable skills and experience, just what skills are in the highest demand?
The Top 5 In-Demand Tech Skills
The job board, Indeed.com, released a list of its top 10 highest-paid skills within the tech industry, which are raking in some of the highest salaries advertized on the platform.
If you're already within tech, or desire to transition into the industry, have a look below at five of these skills so you can plan your next career move accordingly this year. Some of these skills may be relevant for you to help you stand out as a professional or leader in your field, even if you're not in the technology industry.
1. Generative AI
That's right, you guessed it. Generative AI stands at the foremost of the highest-income tech skills on Indeed's list. Some skills related to this include prompt engineering, ChatGPT, Midjourney, model tuning, AI content creation, and even data analytics. This skill boasts an estimated 47% salary bump, according to Indeed's analysis.

SoC means "system-on-chip" and it is "an integrated circuit that integrates most or all components of a computer or other electronic system," according to the report. Resources such as Arm provide useful course materials on GitHub to help you learn the fundamentals of this technical skill. The income potential for someone with this skill is $175k per annum.

Deep learning is the foundation of artificial intelligence and a subset of machine learning. It is so called due to the multiple layers in the network, in which complicated patterns are learned from lower-level, simpler ones. Having this skill can make up to a 44% difference in your salary, and demand will continue as AI continues to be implemented and developed, so it's definitely worth considering upskilling so you can add to your tool kit.

Learning Torch can place you at a 43% salary advantage.

Computer vision is another skill closely related to the field of artificial intelligence, and it involves "enabling computers to identify and understand objects and people in images and videos. Like other types of AI, computer vision seeks to perform and automate tasks that replicate human capabilities," says Microsoft.
Computer vision allows an application to gain a high-level understanding of the physical world, extract meaningful information, and make decisions from them. One such example of computer vision in an application would be the facial recognition on your phone. Online providers, such as Stanford Online, deliver computer vision courses. This skill has the potential to yield up to a 40% increase in your salary.

Getty-backed AI image generator BRIA snags fresh funding
The investment, while small relative to others in the white hot AI space, makes BRIA an early test case in how licensing deals can provide a path forward in disputes raging over the use of copyrighted content to train generative AI models.
By Katie Paul
NEW YORK: A "responsible" AI image generation startup backed by stock photo provider Getty Images has raised $24 million in a Series A funding round, including from top ad agency Publicis Groupe, it said on Wednesday.
Israel-based BRIA, which licenses more than a billion images from stock providers for its system, said in a press release that it would use the cash infusion to expand globally and build out text-to-video generation capabilities.
The investment, while small relative to others in the white hot AI space, makes BRIA an early test case in how licensing deals can provide a path forward in disputes raging over the use of copyrighted content to train generative AI models.
Music labels, artists and other content owners have pointed to licensing as a more palatable approach to generative AI, after big AI companies built their systems using content scraped off the open internet for free.
BRIA said its license-only approach heads off the risk of trademarks and other fraught elements appearing in its generated images, attracting customers in the advertising, marketing and media world including Publicis.
"There is a way to do this that is both responsible and commercial," CEO Yair Adato told Reuters in an interview.
Getty, which has backed BRIA since 2022, has figured prominently in the disputes around training data.
Last year, Getty sued leading AI image generation company Stability AI for using its photos without a license, which it alleged was "brazen" infringement of its intellectual property "on a staggering scale."
It also teamed up with chip maker Nvidia last year to build an image generation service trained only on the images in its own library.
Rivals Adobe and Shutterstock likewise offer AI image generators, while all three photo companies license their visuals to Nvidia for its own service.
BRIA fed its model visuals from 18 stock providers, including Getty, Alamy, SuperStock and Envato. It charges customers for access to the platform and shares revenue with the photo companies.
Each time BRIA generates an image, it displays the original licensed images that contributed data toward that output and accounts for how much came from each.
Adato likens the approach to a Spotify model for the AI era, which compensates content owners for their role in enabling the technology.
Controlled training also guards against the technology being used to create misleading visuals that could tarnish brands or influence elections, he said.
BRIA's model, for instance, is not capable of generating an image of U.S. President Joe Biden because it has never been taught what he looks like, said Adato.

text:

Google releases 'open' AI models after Meta
The move may attract software engineers to build on Google's technology and encourage usage of its newly profitable cloud division. The models are "optimized" for Google Cloud, where first-time cloud customers using them get $300 in credits, the company said.
SAN FRANCISCO: Google on Wednesday released new artificial intelligence (AI) models that outside developers potentially can fashion as their own, following a similar move by Meta Platforms and others.
The Alphabet subsidiary said individuals and businesses can build AI software based on its new family of "open models" called Gemma, for free. The company is making key technical data such as what are called model weights publicly available, it said.
The move may attract software engineers to build on Google's technology and encourage usage of its newly profitable cloud division. The models are "optimized" for Google Cloud, where first-time cloud customers using them get $300 in credits, the company said.
Google stopped short of making Gemma fully "open source," meaning the company still may have a hand in setting terms of use and ownership. Some experts have said open-source AI was ripe for abuse, while others have championed the approach for widening the set of people who can contribute to and benefit from the technology.
With the announcement, Google did not make its bigger, premier models known as Gemini open, unlike Gemma. It said the Gemma models are sized at two billion or seven billion parameters - or the number of different values that an algorithm takes into account to generate output.
Meta's Llama 2 models range from seven to 70 billion parameters in size. Google has not disclosed the size of its largest Gemini models. For comparison, OpenAI's GPT-3 model announced in 2020 had 175 billion parameters.
Chipmaker Nvidia on Wednesday said it has worked with Google to ensure Gemma models run smoothly on its chips. Nvidia also said it will soon make chatbot software, which it is developing to run AI models on Windows PCs, work with Gemma.

title: Council Post: Open-Source AI For Image Generation: Strategies For Startups
text:
Runde Yang is co-founder of Dream Voyage, building in AI and gaming.
The rapid democratization of artificial intelligence has led to the development of image-generation tools powered by open-source models and code. Models like Stable Diffusion and web user interfaces such as Automatic1111 give users the power to craft intricate digital art with no coding required. As AI research and development increasingly occurs in public view, I believe the future trajectory points toward more innovations sprouting from nonproprietary toolkits anyone can access.
My company has close ties to open-source image models. We have built an AI-powered dream interpretation app in which we use open-source image models to visualize users' dreams. Based on my experience, I believe that for new startups aiming to ride this wave, open collaboration rather than closed competition can provide opportunities. By understanding the ethos and unique advantages of open source in AI image creation, new companies can strategically position themselves for sustainable success.
Why Startups Might Consider Open Source
I believe there are fundamental reasons why open development has become so prolific. These structural incentives will likely only solidify over time. Here are some of the benefits of using open-source technology that startups should consider:
Accelerated Community Knowledge
One major benefit of public development is the combination of insights from a diverse set of contributors. I've seen research labs publish experiments on open platforms ranging from algorithmic tweaks to full models. Teams can build on top of one another’s code, reproduce results and extend functionality often faster than closed efforts, in my experience. The bring-your-own-model culture of sharing breeds direct replication of cutting-edge advances that proprietary groups wouldn't reveal behind closed doors.
Wider Engagement And Feedback
In addition to researchers, I've observed open-source AI image tools attract interest from casual users, artists, developers, student hobbyists and industry specialists alike. This engagement spectrum can give public projects unique feedback and testing data to improve rapidly. Closed solutions, in my experience, rarely achieve this level of diverse real-world validation during product development cycles.
The raw engagement energy I've observed in some open-source communities highlights the buy-in people feel when directly participating in an open stack they help build. The number of models and LoRA uploaded to platforms such as Hugging Face and Civitai form millions of combinations for image-generation options. These can range from photorealistic models, such as Realistic Vision, to animation models, such as Anything V3.
Lower Barriers To Entry
For entrepreneurs with limited startup resources, building atop publicly available building blocks can provide efficiency advantages. Some technical obstacles around data, model training and infrastructure can be bypassed by pulling directly from open repositories and leveraging available programs.
Efforts can then shift more to designing interfaces, targeted niche functionality and impactful custom use cases rather than reinventing foundational elements. I believe apps like Photoroom, an AI photo editor that is reportedly raising between $50 million and $60 million in funding, according to Techcrunch, demonstrate the power of narrow specialization made possible by open foundations.
Focusing On User Experience
As underlying AI imaging technology increasingly commoditizes through open development, the biggest opportunities lie in creating delightful user experiences. As I see it, the greatest needs exist not in core model training but in building intuitive interfaces, seamless workflows and instantiated vertical use cases. Making open algorithms accessible and helpful for human needs is where sustainable value can be added.
Consider ComfyUI, which layers a transparent user interface/user experience design on top of Stable Diffusion capabilities. This shows a focus on the human experience. I believe infinite niche segments and stand-alone apps are waiting for a specialized approach on top of universally available imaging engines.
The Future Is Open
Recent industry debate highlights concerns about the power concentration held by large private companies training proprietary foundation models. In the context of this concern, I think open source can act as a check toward democratization. On the creative side, I believe models like Latent Diffusion may point toward fully decentralized, community-hosted options.
As barriers to access continually lower, I expect global participation from student hobbyists to corporate behemoths will further accelerate open collaboration. Whether through code contributions, detailed bug finding, specialized use cases or direct model training, diverse engagement could birth tremendous innovation that might be bottlenecked within closed walls.
Strategies For Startups
New companies aiming to surf this wave of open AI abundance must embrace the unique ethos of transparency and decentralization that defines this space. Attempting to hoard IP or keeping secrets will only hamper the influx of external support possible in public domains. Instead, some forward-looking principles include:
• Actively participate in relevant open communities by sharing insights, code, data and experiments whenever possible. Doing so builds valuable relationships and trust.
• Strategically determine what parts of the stack require proprietary control based on business models. Is closed data or a secret sauce algorithm necessary, or is it just notional clinging to old defaults?
• Consider leveraging publicly available resources so efforts can focus squarely on delightful user experiences instead of re-creating base models.
• Openly credit and highlight communities and researchers that empower your offerings so all ships rise together.
However, startups should also keep in mind that open-source models might exhibit risks in content moderation. Certain community models are uncensored and can potentially create harmful content. Therefore, startups must pay extra caution over the training set of open-source models and make sure appropriate content moderation is applied before rolling out to end users.
By embracing the collaborative power of open-source AI image generation, startups can ride tremendous momentum rather than struggle against the tide. I believe the future points clearly toward democratization, which savvy entrepreneurs can harness for outsized opportunities relative to playing alone in closed silos. From my view, the collective energy emerging promises a Cambrian explosion of creative tools once bottled up in private; companies just need to embrace the collaborative ethos fueling it all.

title: Council Post: From Script To Distribution: AI's Role In The Film World
text:
Dr. Ayesha Khanna is the CEO of Addo.
From R2-D2 of Star Wars to Ultron of The Avengers, the "reel" world has long been fascinated with AI. But in today's cinema, AI isn't just a character; it's a behind-the-scenes maestro.
From conceiving the idea to final distribution, the “AI in entertainment and media” market is projected to reach $132.16 billion by 2032.
Here's how AI is influencing multiple phases of filmmaking.
AI In Pre-Production
AI is applied in pre-production for script analysis, as exemplified by companies like StoryFit. It uses AI to analyze scripts, characters and audience responses, offering studios valuable insights.
For instance, StoryFit's analysis revealed communication patterns between male and female characters in films, providing insights for improving character dynamics and dialogue. They examined zombie-related films like HBO’s Last of Us to understand how socio-political events influence the horror genre, offering insights for filmmakers tackling current societal themes.
AI also supports the scriptwriting process, with tools like Pickaxe aiding writers in generating scenes by prompting plot and character descriptions into a text box. While the output may not be a final draft, it serves as a creative spark, providing inspiration.
Moreover, AI can predict key elements of a film's success, such as box office revenue and audience preferences. Warner Bros., for instance, collaborates with AI platforms like Cinelytic to guide choices on release dates, marketing and distribution. Cinelytic's forecasting proved accurate with Hellboy, closely aligning with the film's actual box office performance.
AI In Production
In cinematography, AI offers assistance in executing precise camera movements, scene optimizations for ideal lighting and composition, and suggesting adjustments for enhanced visuals and shot composition. AXIBO, for example, pioneers AI-powered camera automation, providing noise-free motion and diverse control options.
Another tool, Move.ai, employs AI for markerless 3D motion capture, eliminating the need for actors in traditional motion capture suits. This innovation is particularly significant as it allows remote motion capture.
AI enhances real-time special effects, like Massive software simulating lifelike crowd behaviors in movies such as the Battle of Helm's Deep in The Lord of the Rings. This technology uses AI to create realistic computer-generated armies, aiding cinematic battles.
AI In Post-Production
Post-production tasks, such as editing, special effects, audio editing and soundtracks, are often technical and time-consuming. AI has the potential to streamline these processes by automating repetitive tasks.
AI tools like Blackmagic Design's DaVinci Neural Engine leverage ML algorithms to adjust color tone, remove noise and track objects across footage, considerably reducing the time and effort required for post-production tasks.
Another notable AI tool, Runway ML is used by VFX artists for tasks such as inpainting, motion tracking, greenscreen, and object/background removal, streamlining manual processes. This was used in the award-winning film Everything Everywhere All At Once for background and visual effects.
Similarly, Wonder Dynamics' AI tool, Wonder Studio, automates actor-to-CG character replacement, managing animation, lighting and composition in real time. This innovation democratizes CGI and VFX for small budgets, freeing artists to concentrate on creativity over technical tasks.
De-aging actors is gaining popularity, with companies like Metaphysic providing AI alternatives to traditional VFX and CGI.
In a video showcasing a de-aged Harrison Ford in Cowboys & Aliens, AI tracked and diffused his face every 30th frame using Stable Diffusion, presenting a more efficient and cost-effective approach compared to CGI-heavy methods seen in films like The Irishman.
AI goes beyond visuals—it's handy for audio editing, too. Izotope's Neutron software, featuring Track Assistant and Mix Assistant, analyzes and creates custom presets to enhance audio tracks. This provides a solid starting point for audio mixers, significantly reducing editing time.
Marketing And Distribution
AI recommendation engines improve viewer satisfaction by personalizing content suggestions on platforms like Netflix. The company continually refines its algorithms through user data, studying viewing habits and analyzing platform interactions.
AI is also playing a role in trailer creation. For instance, in 2016, IBM Watson used AI to craft a trailer for Morgan by analyzing key film moments, suggesting soundtracks and refining edits. In 2019, Adobe Sensei analyzed past Sundance Film Festival winners, using AI to create an original short film that captured the festival's essence.
Ethical Considerations
While AI leads to benefits, from cost and time savings to improved outputs and aid in creativity, it is not without its concerns.
A significant concern is the potential bias in AI-generated content. AI algorithms learn from data, and if that data is biased, the content may reinforce stereotypes and marginalize certain groups. To address this, it's crucial to use diverse and representative training data.
Last year’s 118-day-long joint strike by SAG-AFTRA and the WGA brought attention to intellectual property rights and privacy issues. It focused on AI use and safeguarding actors and writers. Eighty-six percent of the union vote was in favor of AI use, but studios must obtain an actor's consent before digitally emulating them; actors will be paid for the days a digital replica is used in their stead.
Another major concern is determining ownership and royalties for AI-generated content since it challenges existing copyright laws. Recently, it was highlighted by the U.S. judgment announcing that AI-generated content cannot be copyrighted.
AI-generated storytelling sparks concerns about diminishing human touch, originality and creativity, prompting a crucial question: Can these narratives retain relatable flaws and uniqueness, resonating with our shared human experience?
What Comes Next?
As AI-generated short films and stories gain popularity and AI becomes more prevalent in mainstream post-production, it's clear that AI's influence in the film industry will keep growing, paving the way for further innovation.
For example, Pika Labs, an AI video generator, raised $55 million in funding, valued between $200 million and $300 million. The platform, initially focused on anime, now caters to a broader audience, generating AI-created videos based on text inputs.
Picture an AI-powered casting assistant, efficiently recommending actors based on project requirements, a video editor that can make most of your required changes by simply following text prompts or a camera that filters the background and adjusts lightning at the time of shooting using AI; the possibilities are endless.

title: $1 Trillion Question: Will Nvidia Dominate The Coming Ubiquitous AI Era?
text:
George Gilder is confident that “at present, we're in the IBM mainframe era of AI.” This “AI gigantism,” he says, with its big data centers and billion-parameter models, is going to give way to AI “in every smart phone and every pocket, distributed through the internet of things.” As the new technology platform of the age, AI is going to be decentralized, ubiquitous and transformative.
Gilder made these observations last week, at a webinar for the OurCrowd community and the Gilder Private Reserve subscribers. A prolific writer and opinionated investment advisor, for more than forty years Gilder has preached the gospel of decentralization, autonomy, and life after bigness. His convictions cum predictions, while sometimes overstating and overestimating developments in the short term, tracked well the general trajectory of computer-based technologies, from the mainframe to the smartphone, and the digitization of everything.
Responding to Gilder, OurCrowd CEO Jon Medved said that “when you talk a decentralized world, you're going to need new accelerators, like new chips that can handle the low power requirements at the edge.” Edge AI is a fast-growing segment of the semiconductor industry and one of its key players is Hailo, an Israeli startup that was the main feature of the OurCrowd/Gilder webinar.
John Schroeder from the Gilder Private Reserve asked Hailo’s CEO Orr Danon to explain the recent developments in computing. AI represents a new approach to computing, Danon answered, in which learning from examples substitutes for traditional programs that provide the computer with a very specific set of instructions. This fundamental change is “an opportunity for a new player to come and take a significant market share,” said Danon.
Rethinking the traditional computer architecture, Hailo invented an AI processor enabling smart devices to perform sophisticated deep learning tasks with minimal power consumption, size, and cost. Hailo’s specialized processor fits into a multitude of smart machines and devices, including autonomous vehicles, smart cameras, smartphones, drones, AR/VR platforms, and wearables.
“Technologies like ours make it possible for applications to proliferate from the cloud to near where data is produced and consumed. If you're doing anything that requires a quick response, you have to be local,” said Danon.
The processing of data in the cloud and at the edge works hand-in-hand for AI applications. “Training is the phase where you teach the models what you want them to do. This is something that rarely makes sense in a local context,” Danon explained.
While there are a few edge cases where the knowledge required for training is very specific and local, for the majority of use cases it makes much more sense to do the training of the AI model by using the data that is stored in the cloud. But at the next phase of AI deployment, the inference stage, it makes more sense to do it at the edge. “Hailo is a complementary play to the more power hungry, extreme high-performance direction which Nvidia is taking,” said Danon.
Hailo’s chip not only cost less to manufacture and to buy, but it also requires only one or two watts for power consumption as opposed to an Nvidia chip which requires 60 or 70 watts. “Hailo’s architecture is based on a data flow approach rather than the traditional way CPUs and GPUs have been designed,” said Dannon. As such, it is “more suitable for the way today’s AI is being designed,” with a strong focus on performance benchmarks, both performance per dollar and performance per watt.
At stake is the global market for semiconductors which is projected to reach $1 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey, which predicts that “semiconductors stand to dominate the next decade in global business.” Much of this growth is attributed to the rapid adoption of AI by businesses worldwide, leading to an expected $1 trillion in investment in semiconductor manufacturing capacity from 2023 to 2030. “This frenzy of global expansion could reshape the industry and disperse the balance of power around the world,” says McKinsey.
The projected demand for AI power and Nvidia’s current 80% share of the market for high-end AI chips have invited competition. OpenAI’s Sam Altman, reported the Wall Street Journal, is raising $5 to $7 trillion to boost the world’s chip-building capacity. AMD and Intel are introducing new AI-focused chips. Heavy AI users such as Google and Facebook are developing their own AI chips. And smaller companies are joining the race, such as customized AI servers developer Super Micro.
Nvidia is not sitting still and has responded to the new competition in a variety of ways. It has invested in AI startups. It has established a new business unit focused on designing custom chips for cloud computing firms and other companies, Reuters reports. It recently released Chat with RTX, a locally running AI assistant. Investors are bullish and Nvidia has recently surpassed Amazon and Alphabet to become the third-biggest U.S. company by market value.
Are we witnessing a tipping point, similar to the introduction of the smart phone in 2007? Is this another milestone in the nonstop progression of computer technology from big to small, from the data center to the edge? Is AI (i.e. artificial neural networks or deep learning) a new catalyst, just like the previous inventions of the internet (i.e. the world wide web) and the iPhone were the catalysts for an explosion in the production and consumption of data and a new phase in “data is eating the world”? Should we anticipate another reshuffling of the semiconductor deck, similar to how the near-monopolist Intel stumbled with no adequate response to the rise of mobile?
George Gilder knows the answer: “Nvidia has reached its climactic complexity and is going to give way to companies like Hailo in the future.”

title: Beyond The Crystal Ball: AI's Controversial Power To Predict Our Death Date
text:
The insurance industry, traditionally reliant on statistical models and actuarial tables, is undergoing a significant transformation. With the advent of AI, insurers are exploring new frontiers in risk assessment, including the controversial practice of using AI to predict an individual's death date. This emerging trend raises profound ethical questions and concerns about privacy, discrimination, and the role of technology in our lives.
The Rise of AI in Lifespan Prediction
The core of life insurance is predicting life expectancy. Traditionally, the death date calculation is rooted in factors like age, medical history, lifestyle choices, and family health history. However, the integration of AI and machine learning is shifting this paradigm. By analyzing vast and complex datasets, AI systems can identify patterns and correlations that might elude human analysts. For instance, some insurance companies are experimenting with AI to analyze medical images, such as MRI scans, to detect early signs of life-threatening diseases. Other companies are using wearable technology data to monitor policyholders' health and lifestyle in real-time, potentially offering more accurate life expectancy predictions.
The Impact to You
While specific insurance companies openly using AI to predict death dates are not widely publicized because of the sensitive nature of the subject, there are some known instances of AI being utilized for closely related purposes. For example, John Hancock, one of the largest life insurance providers in the United States, announced in 2018 that it would convert its life insurance offerings into interactive policies using wearable technology and data analytics. This approach includes monitoring fitness and health data through wearable devices, potentially affecting premiums and policy conditions based on the policyholder's lifestyle choices. Then, there is VitalityLife, a UK-based insurance firm, offers a similar program. It provides incentives for healthy behaviors tracked through wearable devices, suggesting a move toward more personalized insurance policies based on AI-driven data analysis.
Ethical and Privacy Concerns
Using AI to predict life expectancy is fraught with ethical challenges. The foremost concern is privacy. Collecting and analyzing detailed health and lifestyle data invade personal privacy, and there are valid concerns about how this data is stored, used, and protected. Another significant concern is discrimination. Bias within AI systems is dependent on the training data they are fed. If the data contains historical or implicit biases, the AI's predictions may be skewed, leading to unfair policy rates or coverage denial for certain groups of people. This raises questions about the fairness and equality of AI-driven life insurance policies. Likewise, the opaque nature of AI algorithms also poses challenges. Policyholders may find it difficult to understand how their rates are calculated or why they might be denied coverage. This lack of transparency can erode trust and raise accountability concerns, especially if the AI makes an erroneous prediction.
Regulatory and Industry Response
Recognizing these challenges, regulators and industry bodies are beginning to respond. Many are calling for stricter guidelines on the use of AI in life insurance, emphasizing the need for transparency, data protection, and ethical considerations. In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides some safeguards, including the right to explanation for decisions made by AI algorithms. Similarly, in the United States, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) is actively discussing the implications of AI and big data in insurance.
Balancing Innovation with Ethical Responsibility
As the insurance industry navigates this new terrain, it's imperative to strike a balance between leveraging AI for more accurate risk assessment and upholding ethical standards. To begin with, insurance companies must develop ethical frameworks for AI use, prioritizing transparency, fairness, and privacy. This involves not just adhering to existing laws but also going beyond them to establish trust with policyholders. More importantly, it's also crucial to involve a diverse range of stakeholders in the development and deployment of AI systems. This includes ethicists, consumer advocates, data scientists, and policyholders themselves. Their insights can help ensure that AI systems are fair, unbiased, and respectful of privacy. Finally, AI systems should not be set and forgotten. Continuous monitoring and improvement are necessary to ensure they remain fair and accurate as new data comes in and as societal norms and regulations evolve.
The Road Ahead
The use of AI in predicting life expectancy for insurance purposes is an area of intense debate and rapid development. While it offers the potential for more accurate risk assessment and personalized policies, it also brings significant ethical challenges that must be addressed. As companies move forward, the insurance industry must navigate these challenges with a commitment to ethical principles, transparency, and the protection of individual rights. The goal should not be to use technology for its own sake but to harness it in ways that serve the greater good and respect the dignity and privacy of individuals.
Ultimately, the intersection of AI and life insurance is a complex and evolving field. It's an area ripe with potential but also fraught with ethical pitfalls. The path forward requires careful consideration, regulatory oversight, and a commitment to ethical practices. As we embrace the possibilities of AI, we must also remain vigilant to ensure that technology serves humanity, not the other way around.

title: Pioneering LLM Applications In Healthcare And The Life Sciences
text:
Peter Leimbigler is a Data Science Team Leader within the Consulting practice at Klick Health. As the largest independent commercialization partner in its industry, Klick pioneers new AI-powered applications for clients across life sciences, pharmaceuticals, medical device, and consumer health to accelerate growth and improve experiences and outcomes for patients and consumers. That’s especially true in the current wave of emerging developments in generative AI. We caught up with Peter to learn more about AI work for clients, large language model (LLM) use cases, and thoughts on the evolving LLM operations (LLMOps) landscape.
Can you introduce yourself, covering your background and your role at Klick Health?
I lead the data science team at Klick Consulting, which helps define and solve complex problems in the healthcare and life sciences space across a wide range of clients – startup to global, at various lifecycle stages. We evaluate and adopt technology to serve business needs, and are excited to be taking an experiment-driven approach to using LLMs effectively and responsibly. This includes staying up to date on models themselves, as well as the blossoming field of LLMOps.
Career-wise, I'm one of those data scientists who pivoted into the role from an adjacent quantitative field. I studied physics as an undergraduate, then earned a Master of Science in Medical Biophysics at the University of Toronto. I used Python and other open-source software to wrangle and analyze complex datasets and brought this experience to interesting problems in industry at Klick.
Data science fulfilled my personal desire to work at the intersection of various different disciplines rather than hyper-specializing. Ultimately, I wanted to make a real impact in the lives of actual people. I was fortunate to be among the first data scientists at Klick, working on a centralized team to address data and advanced analysis needs across the company. I then evolved into my current consulting role where I fit data solutions to client problems while collaborating closely with the advanced analytics and data science functions beyond the Consulting team.
What should people know about Klick Health and why AI is core to what you do?
Klick Health is the world's largest independent commercialization partner for healthcare and life sciences. Data and analytics have always been a pillar of our offerings, from augmenting human experts to work faster, to equipping clients with competitive insights and forecasts.
Within Klick, Klick Consulting is a growth acceleration partner for consumer and prescription based healthcare companies. We integrate strategy and execution, going further than most consultancies to bring our recommendations to market through our team of specialists. AI is a great example of where we have been helping clients. Clients want to use it to solve real problems, but often find themselves working on projects that don't move the needle because of perceived technical or regulatory hurdles.
In the wake of the excitement and investment triggered by ChatGPT's launch, Klick has established a generative AI center of excellence that supports the entire organization to learn how to use AI tools effectively and responsibly, and to support internal and client-facing projects where genAI technology is deployed. This Klick-wide initiative is designed to promote hands-on experience, which we believe is critical for us to learn what is and isn't useful in this fast-moving field.
As an example, Klick has augmented our own internal operations platform with a chat-based feature that allows us to more easily and efficiently ideate, summarize reports, perform research, and analyze or reshape in-house proprietary data. Through this interface, we are learning best practices for how to improve existing workflows, and how to recognize tasks which are a good fit for LLM-based approaches. Chat is an intuitive and natural interface, yet requires training and practice for effective use, which we've intentionally fostered across Klick.
